newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DUTCH ELECTRICITY PRODUCERS AGREE MERGER.
newsitem.headline: DUTCH ELECTRICITY PRODUCERS AGREE MERGER.

text.p: The Netherlands' four electricity producers have agreed to merge within a year to brace themselves for international competition, their umbrella organisation Sep said on Wednesday.
The companies, EPON, EPZ, EZH and UNA, will become the Grootschalig Productiebedrijf (GPB) on January 1, 1998 with a production capacity of around 15,000 mega-watts.

"GPB will be a big player in the Dutch market, but it is really to face the international competition and the liberalising (European) markets," said Sep (Samenwerkende electriciteits-produktiebedrijven) spokeswoman, Irena Carsouw.
The Dutch government appears prepared to allow the move to proceed with the backing of the Minister of Economic Affairs, Hans Wijers.
"Mr Wijers has sent a letter to parliament on the same proposal, saying it is the most logical step," a ministry spokeswoman said.

Wijers says in his letter to the lower chamber: "I believe it is now time to form a large-scale production company. Longer delay will put us in the background of European development. ... This reconstruction cannot come soon enough."

The companies are already informally linked through their umbrella organisation and the proposed merger is not a surprise to the electricity industry. However, it has been resisted by those who claim that it will stifle domestic competition.

"A decision to merge the four central generators could have considerable significance for competition and efficiency. Potential benefits from competition in a European market should be balanced against benefits obtained from maintaining several producers," the International Energy Agency said in its 1996 review of Dutch energy policy.
Sep says competition is set to increase in the coming years as newcomers, alone or in joint ventures with distribution companies, increase.
"Customers will profit from the competition which will emerge within the electricity sector. The distribution sector will remain free and also able to produce," Carsouw said.
However, unions have already criticised the move and the uncertain future of the generating sector's 5,000 employees.
"It was not made clear in the announcement how many people will be working for the new company. Also, there was no talk of setting up a social plan," four unions said in a statement.
They added they will be putting their demands to the employers on Friday.
Each of the four production companies covers a region of the Netherlands. They are owned by a number of regional electricity distribution companies, cities and provincial authorities.

Last June, European Union ministers agreed the first step in liberalising the electricity market by allowing large industrial consumers free range to shop around for the best prices. The deal should open up a quarter of the EU's market for electricity from January 1999 and a third by 2003.
